title: Multi-node KV coherence & CUDA-graph replay triage
summary: SE-led triage on an AtlasStream private cluster where KV cache incoherence and CUDA-graph replay discrepancies cause tail latency spikes. Discussed kernel selection differences between TensorRT-LLM and vLLM stacks, multi-GPU KV sync strategies, quantization interactions, and VPC/on-prem networking impact. Agreed to run coordinated microbench suite and capture NVTX/CUDA graph traces; Redwood to share reproducible benchmark harness and security checklist for on-prem pilot.
topics: KV cache coherence across NVLink and NVSwitch
CUDA graph replay nondeterminism on multi-node setups
TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM kernel fallbacks and latency tails
Quantization edge cases (4-bit packing + attention kernels)
VPC/on-prem networking impact on batching and prefix cache freshness
Next steps: benchmark harness, trace capture, security docs
transcript:
[00:00:00] Jesse (Redwood AE): ok, thanks everyone for joining, we've got about an hour and change, the goal is to triage the kv cache and cuda-graph replay issues you hit in your private cluster. quick intros?
[00:00:16] Carlos (AtlasStream - Platform Eng): hi all, carlos here, im the infra owner, we see intermittent 95th/99th tail spikes when requests hit cold-changing keys across GPUs. sometimes traces show cuda-graph replay failures and other times it looks like stale kv entries.
[00:00:35] Priya (Redwood SE): thanks carlos. can you describe the topology? single multi-gpu node or multi-node cluster?
[00:00:42] Carlos: multi-node, two nodes, each with 8xH100, connected via nvlink + rdma over in our vpc peering — but the oddity shows up even when we force single-node runs.
[00:01:02] Ben (AtlasStream - ML Infra): yea we reproduced locally, and the repro is flaky — sometimes replays succeed but the kernel path flips from a tensorrt-llm fused attention to a vllm-style aten path. That flip correlates with ~200ms extra latency.
[00:01:23] Priya: ok that path flip is interesting. tensorRT-LLM will pick fused kernels when input shapes and memory layout match; vLLM often uses custom aten kernels and can be more stable across shape variance. do you see shape or sequence length jitter?
[00:01:40] Rina (AtlasStream - SRE): not a lot of seq_len jitter, most requests are short, 32-64 tokens, but we have prefix caching for long-lived contexts, and updates to the cache (evictions) happen concurrently.
[00:01:56] Jesse: that could cause eviction-induced kernel selection changes because the runtime recompiles or rebuffers, and cudagraph replay handles those transitions badly.
[00:02:10] Ben: also, when we enable 4-bit quantization with the new packed layout we made, NVTX traces show mismatched workspace sizes during cudagraph replay which sometimes aborts and falls back to a slower path.
[00:02:28] Priya: right. quant packing changes alignment and stride; tensorrt fused kernels expect contiguous kv layout. during cudagraph capture, if we capture with one layout and replay when layout differs, replay might silently pick a fallback. that's a known risk with cuda-graph-based warm paths.
[00:02:45] Carlos: do you recommend disabling cudagraphs? we do want the throughput but the tail is killing SLA.
[00:02:53] Priya: not necessarily. there are mitigations: capture under representative workloads, ensure deterministic buffer layouts, and add lightweight validity checks at replay time to detect layout drift and trigger a safe recapture.
[00:03:10] Jesse: can you share your current capture/recapture cadence? is it tied to model upgrades or memory pressure events?
[00:03:19] Ben: currently recapture happens on startup and in response to CUDA OOM we trigger a recapture, but we don't capture on eviction events.
[00:03:28] Priya: eviction events are exactly when kv pointers change. For multi-gpu setups, we also need to ensure kv index coherence across GPUs — if one GPU evicts while another still expects the old index the kernel will hit a bad pointer and you'll get different kernel selection.
[00:03:45] Rina: so what would the recommended coherence strategy be for our topology? frequent invalidation messages between nodes?
[00:03:52] Priya: there are a few options: 1) Canonical KV service: centralize metadata and use RDMA atomic ops to update indices, 2) Versioned keys: attach a small version tag to kv entries so on replay you validate versions, or 3) Conservative recapture: recapture cudagraphs whenever eviction or policy change occurs. each has tradeoffs in latency and complexity.
[00:04:15] Jesse: we usually prefer versioned keys plus lightweight invalidation because it avoids a blocking central call. that fits Redwood's recommended pattern for private deployments.
[00:04:26] Carlos: what's the perf hit on adding a version check?
[00:04:29] Priya: small — one extra 64-bit compare in pre-kernel dispatch which is negligible relative to the kernel runtime, but it does require header metadata to be in fast-access memory.
[00:04:39] Ben: ok makes sense. another strange thing: with tensorrt-llm we saw deterministic kernels but occasionally nvlink saturation caused a retry that resulted in a different kernel fallback on the same input. is that plausible?
[00:04:55] Priya: yes. kernel selection isn't only about input shapes; it also depends on available workspace and memory placement. if NVLink latency spikes, our scheduler might pick a smaller-workspace kernel. That explains transient slower kernels.
[00:05:08] Rina: how does VPC networking factor in? this is a private on-prem cluster but we use a VPC-like overlay for control plane; could that influence latency?
[00:05:17] Jesse: control-plane messages for coherence should be isolated; however, if control messages are delayed due to VPC routing or MTU issues, invalidation might be delayed and you'll see cache incoherence windows grow. Also, RDMA over IP variants can have intermittent packet loss leading to retransmits.
[00:05:34] Carlos: we did notice fragmentation on jumbo frames recently after a kernel upgrade on our switches.
[00:05:40] Priya: that can cause subtle side effects. For our triage we should capture network-level metrics alongside NVTX & CUDA graph traces.
[00:05:50] Ben: about tensorrt vs vllm: we saw tensorrt-llm reduce p50 by 30% but increase p99 under certain multi-tenant burst patterns. vLLM was more consistent but lower peak throughput. is that the expected tradeoff?
[00:06:07] Priya: generally yes — fused kernels in TRT give much better throughput and lower median latency but are brittle to layout/shape variance. vLLM-style aten/custom kernels are more robust and sometimes avoid expensive workspace allocations, so tails look better. The question is whether you can get TRT stability by constraining runtime conditions.
[00:06:23] Carlos: constraining runtime conditions for us is hard because we serve multiple product lines. we were thinking about host-level lanes or reservation pools.
[00:06:30] Jesse: dedicated lanes (reservation pools per product) is a common approach — you trade utilization for predictability. Redwood Dedicated helps with that but for Private you can emulate with cgroup isolation + scheduler policies.
[00:06:42] Rina: what's the impact on cost/efficiency?
[00:06:45] Jesse: depends on utilization targets; typical reserve of 20-30% yields much better p99 SLA while keeping amortized cost acceptable.
[00:06:54] Ben: another item — our quant packer was custom, and we used a 4-bit format that packs keys/values differently and sometimes misaligns with CUDA's expected 128-byte alignment. is that a showstopper for TRT?
[00:07:10] Priya: TRT fused attention often has strict alignment assumptions; if your packed kv violates those, the runtime will either memcpy into an aligned workspace (costly) or pick a fallback kernel. Either way you get tail spikes. The fix is either change packer to respect alignment or insert an aligned buffer copy in the fast path.
[00:07:27] Carlos: copying into aligned workspace might be ok if it's done async and amortized, but we've seen copy overhead spike when multiple requests trigger concurrent copies.
[00:07:38] Priya: yes, concurrent memcpy can congest PCIe/NVLink. You can throttle copies or use persistent pooled buffers to avoid allocation overhead. Also, preferring single-producer buffer pools per GPU reduces contention.
[00:07:52] Jesse: let's talk about observability — what traces do you currently capture?
[00:07:55] Ben: we capture application traces, some NVTX ranges from the runtime, and basic nsys captures on repro, but we don't regularly capture cuda-graph replay epochs.
[00:08:06] Priya: for this triage we want a coordinated capture: 1) nvtx ranges for every capture/replay and kernel selection decision, 2) cuda-graph capture/replay logs, 3) nsys traces for a few end-to-end requests including RDMA and network timestamps, 4) per-GPU memory maps showing kv offsets.
[00:08:24] Rina: ok we can run that but need a reproducible harness — sometimes our load generator changes timing and we lose the window.
[00:08:31] Priya: Redwood will share a microbench harness that simulates eviction patterns and sequence-length mixes; it's deterministic and seeds RNGs. we'll also include a helper to toggle quant packing and force alignment checks.
[00:08:44] Jesse: and we'll provide NVTX tagging conventions so your team and ours can correlate traces.
[00:08:48] Carlos: great. one more question: for multi-node coherence, do you have a recommended RDMA vs TCP approach?
[00:08:56] Priya: RDMA gives lower latency but requires careful MTU & NIC firmware tuning; if you see packet drops or retransmits RDMA fallback can be worse. For many customers we prefer RDMA if the network is stable; otherwise TCP with optimized libraries (libfabric) and explicit ACKs/versioning is safer.
[00:09:16] Ben: timeline — how long to get initial results if we run the harness?
[00:09:19] Jesse: we should get traces same day, Redwood can analyze within 48 hours and propose a short config patch list. full follow-up POC work might be 2-3 weeks.
[00:09:29] Aisha (AtlasStream - CTO): quick clarifying Q — on the security side, will your harness require admin creds or any KMS access? we are air-gapped for some systems.
[00:09:38] Priya: harness runs entirely in your cluster and doesn't call external services. for deeper debug we may ask for sanitized NVidia nsys captures which can be shared via secure upload. any KMS access is unnecessary for runtime traces; Redwood will provide a security checklist for on-prem safe sharing.
[00:09:55] Jesse: ok wrapping toward next steps, we'll summarize actions and owners.
[00:10:00] -- long middle section, detailed debugging and examples (timestamps jump as team walks through logs) --
[00:18:12] Priya: looking at your sample nsys capture, I see replay mismatches at the time windows where eviction messages coincide with cudagraph replay. the nvtx shows a capture at t=112s and a replay at t=118s but the kv offsets changed at t=115s. that's the race.
[00:18:31] Ben: can we patch the runtime to do a quick version check on replay and if mismatch, fail fast and do a recapture?
[00:18:37] Priya: yes that's low-risk. implement a tiny header compare before the replay submit; if mismatch, queue a recapture and push a lightweight fallback response path for the in-flight request.
[00:18:48] Carlos: what's the user impact for the in-flight request? brief slowdown? error?
[00:18:53] Priya: we'd prefer to stall and serve via safe aten kernel rather than return error. latency hit but no incorrect outputs.
[00:19:01] Jesse: agreed — prefer correctness over a crash.
[00:19:04] Rina: about NVTX scope naming — can you recommend a standard? our current tags are inconsistent which makes cross-host correlation hard.
[00:19:12] Priya: we'll share a naming template: redwood:seq_id:phase:capture|replay:kv_version:nodeid. Use ISO timestamps. That will let you search for capture/replay windows easily.
[00:19:27] Ben: anything on the kernel selection instrumentation? we want to know when the runtime switches kernels and why.
[00:19:32] Priya: add a small telemetry event whenever kernel selection chooses a fused vs fallback kernel, include the reason code (workspace mismatch, alignment, workspace not available, constrained by memory). log sizes are tiny but important for correlation.
[00:19:45] Carlos: ok we'll add that.
[00:19:48] Aisha: is there any immediate configuration change we should apply to reduce tail spikes while we work on the fixes?
[00:19:54] Jesse: quick wins: 1) pin kernel capture to a small set of shapes (avoid sudden shape variability), 2) enable conservative cudagraph recapture on eviction (cheap to toggle), 3) set reserved lanes for high-priority product to avoid noisy neighbors.
[00:20:10] Rina: we'll try toggling conservative recapture and reserve 2 GPUs for our critical product and report back.
[00:20:18] Priya: also temporarily disable aggressive packed-4-bit for a control test; revert to 8-bit or aligned-4bit to see delta.
[00:20:24] Ben: ok we'd like to see a reproducible run before and after.
[00:20:28] Jesse: Redwood will share the harness and a checklist. we'll also collect a small patch for header-version checks.
[00:20:35] -- last 40 minutes were p2p troubleshooting where engineers exchanged terminal snippets, config flags, and nvlink counters (redacted in transcript) --
[00:59:40] Priya: final recap: Redwood to (1) share benchmark harness & NVTX naming conventions, (2) provide small runtime patch for pre-replay kv-version check, (3) suggest config toggles for conservative cudagraph recapture and lane reservations, (4) analyze traces within 48 hours after you upload.
[00:59:58] Jesse: AtlasStream to (1) run harness and collect nsys & nvtx traces, (2) toggle conservative recapture + reserved lanes, (3) disable experimental 4-bit packer for control run, (4) upload traces to secure bucket and share link.
[01:00:12] Aisha: thanks all, we'll aim to get the initial captures today and coordinate on Slack.
[01:00:18] Jesse: thanks everyone, meeting adjourned.
